title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether middle school students can regulate inquiry effectively when using ChatGPT for science investigation tasks. The authors focus on three aspects of interaction quality: discriminating between efficient and inefficient prompts, evaluating the usefulness of AI-generated answers, and deciding whether to continue asking follow-up questions or terminate the inquiry cycle. The broader motivation is to understand over-reliance, poor epistemic vigilance, and the potential for AI to create an “illusion of understanding” in K-12 learners.

The study involved 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 from four schools in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region. Students completed questionnaires on AI attitudes and metacognition, then worked through six science inquiry tasks during a one-hour session with unrestricted access to ChatGPT 3.5. For each task, they judged a suggested prompt as efficient or inefficient, interacted with ChatGPT, rated every answer they received, and submitted a final written explanation in their own words. Researchers analyzed logs, ratings, and final responses, comparing student judgments with expert-coded answer quality.

Results showed that students were generally unable to reliably distinguish efficient from inefficient prompts and were similarly poor at evaluating whether AI responses were informative. Follow-up questioning was rare, indicating weak regulation of the inquiry cycle, and task success was only moderate. Positive attitudes toward AI and higher confidence in prior domain knowledge were associated with worse calibration, while metacognitive regulation and more critical views of AI predicted better interaction quality. The authors conclude that students need explicit AI literacy instruction focused on metacognitive regulation and critical evaluation, not just technical familiarity with generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical observational study with quantitative analyses, but it is not an experiment or randomized comparison, and the authors themselves note limitations such as small sample size and reliance on correlational/path analyses. It provides useful evidence, but internal validity is limited for causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests meaningful negative effects of unscaffolded ChatGPT use on K-12 inquiry quality, overreliance, and conceptual understanding, but the observed academic impact is modest-to-unclear overall (e.g., success rate 0.51) and based on a small sample. It is important for priority populations, but the direct effect size evidence is not strong enough for a higher impact tier.

interventions.use_case: Middle-school students used ChatGPT 3.5 as a conversational science inquiry support for unrestricted question-asking, prompt selection, answer evaluation, and follow-up questioning across six science investigation tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Students using ChatGPT for science inquiry showed only moderate task success, with an average correct solution rate of Msuccess=0.51 (SD=0.25) across six problems (n=63). Although high-level AI answers were associated with better outcomes, students’ inability to reliably discriminate prompt quality (Md′=0.19, t=1.77, p=0.08) and answer quality (Md′=0.07, t=-0.45, p=0.65) limited their ability to build accurate conceptual explanations.
finding.measure: Binary-coded written science explanations judged as deep, clear, explicitly addressing the problem, and accurate (success rate across six tasks)

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong evidence of weak metacognitive regulation during LLM-supported inquiry: prompt discrimination was at chance (Md′=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08), answer discrimination was also at chance (Md′=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65), and only 14 of 63 students asked any follow-up questions. Positive AI attitudes and prior domain knowledge were associated with worse sensitivity to prompt or answer quality, indicating overreliance and poor epistemic vigilance.
finding.measure: Signal detection sensitivity to prompt quality and answer quality; follow-up-question frequency; correlations/regressions with metacognition and AI attitudes
finding.effect_size: Md′=0.19 for prompt discrimination; Md′=0.07 for answer discrimination; β values reported for predictors (e.g., β=-.39, β=-.35, β=.3)
finding.std_deviation: SD=0.8 for prompt d′; SD=1.2 for answer d′

finding.finding_summary: The interaction patterns suggest over-reliance and premature termination of inquiry rather than sustained engagement. Only 14 students generated follow-up questions (22 total across six tasks), and students often accepted or reused prompts they had judged inefficient, indicating low persistence in the QA cycle despite unrestricted access to ChatGPT.
finding.measure: Follow-up-question frequency; prompt acceptance/termination behavior; task completion patterns
